outline.title: Abstract
outline.description: This section provides a concise summary of the entire survey, highlighting the rapid evolution of LLM security threats and defenses between 2023 and 2026. It will outline the shift from static, unimodal vulnerabilities to dynamic, multimodal, and agentic attack vectors. The abstract will briefly touch upon the four core threat categories analyzed: Data and Model Poisoning, Adversarial Attacks, Prompt Injection, and LLM Hallucinations. It will also summarize the survey's contributions, including the systematization of testing methodologies and the proposal of future research directions in co-evolutionary adversarial dynamics.

outline.title: Introduction
outline.description: The introduction establishes the motivation and scope of the survey, framing the critical importance of LLM security in the context of their widespread deployment in high-stakes domains. It will detail the chronological evolution of the field from 2023 to 2026, illustrating the transition from identifying baseline vulnerabilities to navigating a highly sophisticated arms race. The section will outline the survey's structure, explicitly defining the scope to include training-time threats (poisoning), inference-time threats (adversarial attacks, prompt injection), and output integrity issues (hallucinations). It will conclude with a summary of the paper's core contributions to the Nature/ACL-level discourse.

outline.title: Background and Preliminaries
outline.description: This section provides the foundational knowledge necessary to understand the subsequent threat categories. It will define key terminology and provide an overview of modern LLM and Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) architectures. Crucially, it will formalize the threat model, distinguishing between training-time vulnerabilities (e.g., RLHF manipulation) and inference-time exploits. The section will also discuss the underlying alignment and retrieval mechanisms that make modern AI systems functional but simultaneously introduce new attack surfaces, setting the stage for the detailed threat analyses.

outline.title: Training-Time Threats: Data and Model Poisoning
outline.description: This section explores the 2024-2025 evolution of data and model poisoning, highlighting the alarming shift from unimodal text-based vulnerabilities to complex, multimodal, and embodied AI attack vectors. It will detail foundational 2024 studies, specifically referencing [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking] and [Li_2024_Backdoorllm], which benchmarked generative backdoors in open-source models like LLaMA-2, Mistral, and GPT-J. The discussion will then transition to late 2024/2025 developments, focusing on how attackers exploit alignment and retrieval mechanisms, particularly highlighting vulnerabilities within the Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) pipeline, which was traditionally viewed as a safety mechanism.

outline.title: Inference-Time Threats I: Adversarial Attacks
outline.description: Focusing on the 2024-2026 timeframe, this section analyzes the evolution of adversarial attacks from domain-specific vulnerabilities to a sophisticated arms race. It will examine the baseline vulnerabilities of LLMs in high-stakes sectors, prominently featuring [Yang_2024_Adversarial]'s demonstration of model manipulation using sensitive healthcare datasets like MIMIC-III. The section will explore the transition from early patchwork vulnerabilities to advanced offensive weaponization, detailing how attackers craft adversarial inputs to bypass standard model processing, and setting up the context for the defensive strategies discussed later in the survey.

outline.title: Inference-Time Threats II: Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking
outline.description: This section covers the rapid transformation of prompt injection and jailbreak attacks between 2025 and 2026. It will document the definitive shift from static, rule-based bypasses to a dynamic, automated, and co-evolutionary adversarial arms race. The text will detail the application of advanced optimization techniques, including modified Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG), Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) fuzzing, and genetic algorithms. It will explicitly reference the works of [Zhan_2025_LLM], [Wang_2025_LLM], and [Maloyan_2025_LLM], highlighting their success in achieving Attack Success Rates (ASR) of 50% to 71% against state-of-the-art LLM agents in both black-box and agentic environments.

outline.title: Model Reliability: LLM Hallucinations and Factual Consistency
outline.description: This section traces the 2023-2026 evolution of LLM hallucination detection and mitigation. It will describe the shift from computationally expensive detection to highly optimized, mechanistically informed frameworks. A key focus will be the 2023 landmark introduction of zero-shot inference-time methods, specifically detailing ChainPoll [Friel_2023_LLM], which utilized LLM-based polling and Chain-of-Thought prompting to drastically reduce inference costs while outperforming competitors. The section will also cover the 2024 conceptual maturation of the field, where researchers moved beyond treating all non-factual generations as simple binary errors, adopting more nuanced, conceptually rigorous evaluation paradigms.

outline.title: Cross-Cutting Defenses and Mitigation Strategies
outline.description: This section provides a holistic overview of defensive strategies, tracking the evolution from early 'patchwork' external wrappers to integrated, dynamic systems. It will highlight 2024's focus on stateful detection mechanisms and prompt-level manipulations, prominently featuring [Wang_2024_Advqdet]'s contrastive prompt tuning, which achieved up to 99% detection rates against query-based black-box attacks. The discussion will then advance to late 2025/2026 trends, exploring the bifurcation of defenses into two trajectories: the pursuit of extreme computational efficiency and the development of dynamic, ensemble-based systems designed to counter automated, co-evolutionary prompt injection and poisoning threats.

outline.title: Testing Methodologies and Evaluation Frameworks
outline.description: MANDATORY dedicated section synthesizing the evaluation paradigms across all threat categories. It will detail the specific benchmarks, datasets, and metrics used to quantify LLM security. The section will cover the use of specialized datasets like MIMIC-III for domain-specific adversarial testing, and the benchmarking of open-source models (LLaMA-2, Mistral, GPT-J) for poisoning. It will critically analyze key metrics, such as Attack Success Rates (ASR) ranging from 50-71% in prompt injection, and detection rates up to 99% in adversarial defenses. Furthermore, it will evaluate the automated tools driving the offensive state-of-the-art, including MCTS fuzzing and GCG, providing a holistic view of how the community measures security.

outline.title: Discussion and Open Challenges
outline.description: This section synthesizes the broader implications of the survey's findings, identifying critical gaps and limitations in the current state-of-the-art. It will discuss the fundamental inadequacy of static defenses against adaptive optimization techniques and the open challenge of securing multimodal and embodied AI systems against complex poisoning. The discussion will also address the tension between computational efficiency and robust security, proposing future research directions that embrace co-evolutionary adversarial dynamics and mechanistically informed alignment strategies.

outline.title: Conclusion
outline.description: The conclusion provides a final synthesis of the survey, reiterating the paradigm shift from isolated vulnerabilities to a complex, automated adversarial landscape in LLM security. It will offer practical recommendations for researchers and practitioners, emphasizing the necessity of integrated, dynamic defense mechanisms and rigorous, standardized testing methodologies to ensure the safe deployment of next-generation foundation models.
